clue.text: Noted Branch, not retrograde, of Rutland

parts.note: a bough is a large branch of a tree

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so the little word not is read from its end

parts.note: taken as written before being turned

explanation.surface: A celebrated family line from the county of Rutland, which apparently does not go backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrograde' turns NOT into TON. The definition is a name: Rutland Boughton was an English composer, and 'Noted' hints at his music (notes) rather than giving letters; Rutland is also a small English county, which sends the solver to geography.
explanation.definitionFit: Rutland Boughton, the English opera composer, carried that surname, so the surname is the one belonging to Rutland.

clue.text: Fits of amnesia are safest for the 14

definitions.meaning: moments when the mind goes empty
cartridges with no bullet are the least dangerous for a shooter too quick on the trigger

explanation.surface: Losing memory is the safe option for someone too ready to fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is TRIGGER-HAPPY; dummy rounds with no shot are the safe load for such a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Memory lapses are empty spaces in the mind, and empty cartridges carry no bullet, so are harmless.

clue.text: Manchester: footballers turn it loose

indicators.note: turn means the two letters of the word it in the club name are swapped round

parts.note: Manchester United is the famous football club

explanation.surface: Manchester's football team set something free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn it' turns IT round inside UNITED. The definition is an adjective: a knot that has come untied is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfastened knot or lace is no longer tight, so it hangs free.

clue.text: His race is framed from start to finish

definitions.text: His race is framed from start to finish

parts.words: His race is framed from start to finish
parts.note: sounds like a fixed race or a criminal set-up, but the frames are the barriers set across the track all the way along

explanation.surface: A runner's contest was rigged from beginning to end.
explanation.walkthrough: Hurdles are wooden frames; 'framed' suggests a rigged or set-up event.
explanation.definitionFit: This athlete runs a race over barriers placed along the whole length of the course.

clue.text: A deep study

parts.note: sounds like profound thought, but the deep is the sea and the study is scientific

explanation.definitionFit: The science of the seas is literally a study of the deep, the poetic name for the sea.

clue.text: Link with love

parts.note: to join things is to fasten them, and a person who loves someone is said to be fastened to them by affection

explanation.surface: A romantic bond between two people.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to fasten or connect, and its past participle describes someone fond of another, so it links by affection too.

clue.text: An imposter, said Kipling

parts.note: Kipling's poem If advises meeting success and disaster and treating those two impostors just the same

explanation.surface: Rudyard Kipling calls someone a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines are from Kipling's poem 'If—': 'If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two impostors just the same'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's poem names great success as one of two impostors, alongside Disaster.

clue.text: Hill-dweller run away with his dear, deerie me !

parts.note: an ant lives in an anthill
to elope is to run off secretly with a lover

explanation.surface: A highlander runs off with his sweetheart, to an old Scots exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hill-dweller' suggests a mountain creature, but it is the anthill's resident. The definition plays on 'dearie me': the animal is deer-like, though not a true deer.
explanation.definitionFit: This horned grazing animal looks much like a deer, so it is something deer-ish.

clue.text: Oldish, ay — but how we go for them !

definitions.text: Oldish, ay — but how we go for them !

indicators.note: go here is read as come apart and change order, as letters do when shuffled

explanation.surface: A middle-aged speaker admits to age but still loves getting away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go' rearranges OLDISH AY, and the whole clue describes breaks people take eagerly however old they get.
explanation.definitionFit: Vacations are the times away people go off on and eagerly go for.

clue.text: Routes that make one sanguine of the traffic problem?

definitions.text: Routes that make one sanguine of the traffic problem?

parts.words: Routes that make one sanguine of the traffic problem?
parts.note: main roads relieve traffic, but sanguine also means of blood, so these are the body's main routes for blood traffic

explanation.surface: A town planner hopes new main roads will cheer motorists about congestion.
explanation.walkthrough: Sanguine means hopeful but comes from the Latin for blood; major trunk roads are called arterial roads.
explanation.definitionFit: The vessels carrying blood away from the heart are the body's main highways, which is why trunk roads borrow their name.

clue.text: One who might become 14 in the Boar's Head tavern?

definitions.text: One who might become 14 in the Boar's Head tavern?

parts.words: One who might become 14 in the Boar's Head tavern?
parts.note: the Boar's Head is Falstaff's tavern in Shakespeare's Henry IV, where a swaggering ensign shares his name with a firearm, which might well be too quick on the trigger

explanation.surface: A drinker at a Shakespearean inn who might get too ready to shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is TRIGGER-HAPPY. In Henry IV Part 2 Ensign Pistol brawls in the Boar's Head tavern in Eastcheap; a firearm of that name is the thing that is trigger-happy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespeare character is named after a small handgun, and a handgun is exactly what fires too readily.

clue.text: No revolutions afoot for one who is easy-going

definitions.meaning: a cyclist coasting does not turn the pedals with the feet

explanation.surface: Peace reigns for a relaxed person, with no uprising on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutions afoot' suggests coming rebellions; it means pedal turns of the feet on a bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: Coasting on a bike without pedalling, and living a carefree, unconstrained life, share the same compound.

clue.text: Once the end of a scrambled line to Mr. K.

definitions.text: Once the end of a scrambled line to Mr. K.

parts.note: the initial K, used as written

indicators.note: scrambled means jumbled, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: the abbreviation for mister, used as written

explanation.surface: A coded telephone hotline that once ran to Mr Khrushchev in Moscow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrambled' rearranges LINE with MR K. Mr K was Nikita Khrushchev, the Soviet leader, and the hot line from Washington ended at his seat of government in Moscow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moscow citadel housed the Soviet government, so it was where a direct line to the Soviet leader terminated.

clue.text: Got the idea there was thunder in the air

definitions.meaning: to see through a trick or find someone out, in British slang

definitions.text: there was thunder in the air
definitions.meaning: thunder made a low rolling sound

explanation.surface: Someone sensed a storm coming when they heard it overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang to be found out is to be 'rumbled'.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to see through a deception and to make a deep rolling noise like distant thunder.

clue.text: Too eager to press for expulsion from chambers

definitions.text: Too eager to press for expulsion from chambers

parts.words: Too eager to press for expulsion from chambers
parts.note: reads as an over-keen campaign to throw someone out of a parliament, but the chambers are those of a gun and the press is a finger on the trigger

explanation.surface: An MP is overzealous in campaigning to have a colleague thrown out of the House.
explanation.walkthrough: The chambers of a revolver hold the cartridges which are expelled when the trigger is pressed; 'chambers' first suggests parliament or barristers' offices.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone too ready to shoot is over-keen to squeeze the firing lever, which forces bullets out of the gun's chambers.

clue.text: Minimum investment for patrons of the pools

definitions.text: Minimum investment for patrons of the pools

parts.words: Minimum investment for patrons of the pools
parts.note: reads as the smallest stake for football pools gamblers, but investment means clothing and the pools are for bathing

explanation.surface: The smallest stake allowed for punters on the football pools.
explanation.walkthrough: The football pools are a British weekly betting game on match results; 'investment' also means what one is dressed in.
explanation.definitionFit: A bathing costume is the scantiest garment people wear to the swimming baths.

clue.text: Lots are so docile

definitions.meaning: auction items are open to offers

explanation.surface: Many people are meek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots' looks like 'many', but it means items in an auction.
explanation.definitionFit: Auction items can receive offers, and a meek person readily does as told.

clue.text: Exculpatory monochrome hung on the line

definitions.meaning: clearing someone of blame, especially by covering up faults
laundry all of one pale colour pegged out to dry

explanation.surface: A clean-sheet verdict hung out like pale laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means covering up misdeeds to clear a name, and literally describes laundry of a single pale colour.

clue.text: Man turns up among slippery types in ornamental coats

indicators.note: among puts one piece inside the other

parts.note: eels are notoriously slippery fish

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up means the word man is written from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A man surfaces among some shifty characters wearing decorative coats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' makes NAM, which goes 'among' EELS. The feed's 'Malaya' is not on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitreous glazes fused onto metal or pottery are decorative surface layers.

clue.text: Doyen of 4 ?

parts.note: 4 is the science of the seas, and the senior figure of the seas is the Roman sea god

explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of the sea is the supreme master of the oceans.

clue.text: Jan. 6 music lover

parts.note: January 6 is Twelfth Night, the Shakespeare comedy whose duke opens it by saying music is the food of love

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys music at Epiphany.
explanation.walkthrough: Twelfth Night falls on 6 January; Duke Orsino's first line is 'If music be the food of love, play on'.
explanation.definitionFit: The duke in Twelfth Night opens the play calling for more music.

clue.text: The first importance — or the second ?

definitions.meaning: weight or significance, as in matters of great weight
a very short time, an instant

explanation.surface: Asking whether something matters first or comes second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The first' and 'the second' refer to the two senses, and 'the second' is also a unit of time.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means significance (of great moment) and also a brief instant of time.

clue.text: Christian's depressing cure for incaution

parts.note: in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress the hero Christian, walking heedlessly, falls into the Slough of Despond, a depressing bog, while a spa treatment in sludge is a cure

explanation.surface: A Christian believer's gloomy remedy for recklessness.
explanation.walkthrough: Christian is the pilgrim in Bunyan's allegory; the Slough of Despond is a mire of despair into which he falls. A spa may prescribe a soak in mud as a cure.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallowing in mud is both a health-spa treatment and what befalls a careless walker who strays into a bog.

clue.text: Fires part of the grass to find one that's useful

indicators.note: the letters are there to find inside the run of clue words, spanning a word join

explanation.surface: Someone burns part of a grass field to see which plant is of use.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'firES PART Of'. Esparto is a tough Mediterranean grass used to make paper and rope, hence 'one that's useful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esparto is a coarse North African and Spanish grass whose fibre is woven into rope and paper.

clue.text: The meat in Heep's pie ?

parts.note: Uriah Heep in Dickens's David Copperfield is ever so humble and drops his aitches, and humble pie was originally made from deer offal

explanation.surface: What filling goes into a Dickens character's pie.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep, the fawning clerk in David Copperfield, calls himself ''umble'. Humble pie was once umble pie, made from the offal (umbles) of a deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Umbles are the edible entrails of a deer, the original filling of what became known as humble pie.

clue.text: I fire gun to smash the image

indicators.note: smashing something breaks it into pieces that come together differently

explanation.surface: A vandal shoots a gun to destroy a statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to smash' rearranges the letters of I FIRE GUN.
explanation.definitionFit: A small statuette is a carved or moulded likeness of a person.

clue.text: Godly tea-totaller ?

parts.note: a teetotaller drinks only tea, so a tea-ist; the word that sounds like that names a believer in God

explanation.surface: A pious person who drinks nothing stronger than tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer said as 'tea-ist' would be one devoted to tea, which is what 'tea-totaller' spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer in a deity is godly, and the word can be heard as a devotee of tea.

clue.text: Cumberland town there's reference to in Goethe's play

indicators.note: in shows one piece placed within another

parts.note: Egmont is Goethe's tragedy about a Flemish count
RE means with reference to, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A town in Cumberland is mentioned in a German play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts RE inside EGMONT. Cumberland was an English county in the north-west, now part of Cumbria.
explanation.definitionFit: Egremont is a small market town in West Cumberland, near the coast.
